title: What should you do after a consulting rejection?
description: A kind, practical guide to handling a rejection from a consulting firm: getting useful feedback, deciding what to work on, and when to apply again.
hook: After a consulting rejection, take a day to be disappointed, ask politely for feedback, then look honestly for the one or two skills that let you down and build a focused plan to fix them before you apply again. It hurts, especially after weeks of preparation, and that is normal. Consulting interviews are hard and places are limited, so a rejection is information to use, not a verdict on you.
body:
Give yourself a day

Feel disappointed. Talk to someone. You do not need to analyse anything on the same day, and decisions made in the first few hours tend to be either too harsh on yourself or too dismissive of what went wrong. Come back to it the next morning.

Ask for feedback

Reply to the recruiter, thank them, and ask whether they can share anything that would help you improve. Keep it short and do not argue with the decision. You might get detailed comments, a short note or nothing at all; policies vary by firm and stage, and all three are normal. Here is a message you can adapt:

Thank you for the opportunity to interview with the team, and for letting me know the outcome. I'd really value any feedback on where I could improve, especially on the case. I plan to keep preparing and would be grateful for any pointers.

If you do get feedback, listen without defending yourself. Write it down word for word, then put it alongside your own notes.

Diagnose the pattern, not the outcome

A single interview does not tell you exactly which skill decided the result. You might have nailed the calculations and still failed to pull them into a recommendation, or produced a good structure but been slow to prioritise. Treat your memory and any recruiter feedback as imperfect evidence, then look for patterns across several cases.

The best tool is a short case log. For each recent case, real or practice, note:

ColumnWhat to write
PromptThe case type and question
First three minutesHow your recap, questions and structure went
Data and mathsWhat you asked for, and any calculation errors
RecommendationWas it answer-first, supported and on time?
RedoThe one moment you would do differently

Then look across the rows. If three of your last five cases stalled right after the framework, the problem is not a lack of frameworks. It is driving the case: you need to practise proposing the next step after every finding. The list of common case interview mistakes can help you put a name to what you see.

Make a focused plan

Fix the specific weakness rather than doing more of everything. Match the fix to the problem:

If the problem was...Focus on
Maths errors or slownessTen minutes a day of the case maths drill for a month
Waiting to be told what to doCases where your partner tallies every time you wait instead of leading
Weak or late recommendationsA 60-second answer-first summary at the end of every practice case
Nerves and going blankRecovery drills from the guide to staying calm
The fit interviewRebuilding your story bank and rehearsing follow-ups aloud

A practical reset: spend one week on your weakest skill, then run two unfamiliar cases under timed conditions. Judge improvement by what you can observe, such as fewer missed branches or a correct synthesis within 60 seconds, rather than by how the case felt.

Applying again

Many firms ask unsuccessful candidates to wait before reapplying, and the length can depend on the firm, the office and how far you got. Check the policy directly with the recruiter rather than relying on what others say online. A rejection from one firm does not affect your applications elsewhere, so keep other processes moving. When you do reapply, being able to describe concretely how you have improved since last time is a real strength.

Keep perspective

Consulting is one path among many. The skills you have built preparing for it, structured thinking, clear communication and business sense, are useful wherever you go next. If you decide to try again, you start from a much stronger position than the first time.

Common mistakes

  • Doing more of everything. More cases without a focus repeats the same errors. Target the pattern.
  • Over-reading one comment. A single line of feedback is a clue, not a full diagnosis. Check it against your own log.
  • Arguing with the decision. It will not change the outcome and may affect a future application.
  • Making it a story about your ability. A rejection should sharpen your preparation, not your self-doubt.

Try it now

1. The feedback says "Your structure was good but the case lost momentum." What does that point to, and what would you practise?

Show the answer

Driving the case. Practise ending every finding with a proposed next step: "That tells us costs are the issue, so I'd like to break down costs by type next." Ask a partner to count how often you wait to be told what to do.

2. In your case log, four of six cases had a maths slip, but each was in a different type of calculation. What is the pattern?

Show the answer

Probably not one formula but a habit: rushing, or not sense-checking. The fix is to state your method before calculating and to check the answer against a rough estimate every time, plus daily maths practice.

3. Fill in a case log for your last three cases and name the one skill you will work on this week.

Show the answer

Choose the skill that shows up most often across the "redo" column, not the one that felt worst in a single case. Set one observable target for the week, such as "lead every transition" or "zero unchecked calculations".

Where to practise next

If you have no partner available, use the guide to practising case interviews on your own, and work through realistic cases in the casebook.
